rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verse 74 opens this passage as a prelude to final judgment: messengers testify to their nations’ monotheism before God challenges them to substantiate their alleged partners.
rows.anchor: Here it has come as a prelude to another issue: the Almighty

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The witnesses are God’s messengers, called witnesses because they delivered His religion to their communities in this life and will testify in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: called by this word because they bore witness to God’s religion before their respective

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Later generations bear responsibility for religious innovations they introduced; the messengers who faithfully conveyed God’s religion are absolved.
rows.anchor: innovations in it, it was the latter’s responsibility

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Communities defend polytheism and innovations by attributing them to prophetic teaching, but testimony from those messengers exposes the claim and leaves followers no answer.
rows.anchor: every ummah gives reference to its prophets and messengers: that these beliefs are based on their teachings

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The testimony of messengers is also described in 5:16–17.
rows.anchor: This testimony of the messengers is mentioned in verses 16-17 of

rows.speaker: Imām Ḥamīd al-Dīn Farāhī
rows.claim: Farāhī interprets the verse through 19:69 and 41:47.
rows.anchor: Im ām Ḥam īd al-Dīn Far āhī, interprets this verse in the light of verse 69

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author is unconvinced by Farāhī and prefers the interpretation of other exegetes, which clear Qur’anic parallels support.
rows.anchor: However, I am not convinced of his interpretation.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Earlier, arrogant nations proud of their wealth were destroyed by God, and their deities could not save them.
rows.anchor: by God and their deities who they were proud of could not save them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage resumes the topic from verse 61 after the secondary discussion of polytheism concludes at verse 75; verses 76–84 continue the original theme.
rows.anchor: The succeeding topic is connected to verse 61.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alif Lām Mīm in Luqmān echoes the openings of al-ʿAnkabūt and al-Rūm and signals broadly similar central themes.
rows.anchor: Like the two previous sūrahs (al-‘Ankabūt and al-Rūm), the Qur’ānic name of this one too is Alif Lām Mīm

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Luqmān’s introduction resembles al-Baqarah’s: both identify who will believe in and benefit from the Qur’an and who will remain deprived.
rows.anchor: The introductory part of this sūrah is similar to Sūrah al-Baqarah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Where al-Rūm argued from the world within and around people for a religion aligned with human nature, Luqmān adds the counsel of an Arabian sage to show that past wisdom agrees with the Prophet’s guidance.
rows.anchor: besides arguments drawn from the world around man and that within him, the counsel of Luqma#n, a famous sage of Arabia is alluded to

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Luqmān’s insight shows that common sense accords with the Qur’an and that human nature remains as God created it.
rows.anchor: common sense is in absolute line with what the Qur’ān has mentioned and not what is advocated by the opponents of the Qur’ān

rows.speaker: western philosophers
rows.claim: Western philosophers ground morality in established universal principles founded on common sense.
rows.anchor: western philosophers discuss morality, they base it on established universal principles founded on common sense

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says these philosophers evade a wise Creator and the created nature of humanity, leaving their moral philosophy without a foundation or an account of moral origins.
rows.anchor: they want to evade the concept of a wise creator and of the nature on which God created man

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their theories cannot establish a standard for good and evil or explain why people should do good; proposed utilitarian, happiness, hedonist, and duty-based accounts prove unfounded.
rows.anchor: all proved to be baseless and they themselves proved them to be unfounded

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an grounds both morality and religion in human nature made by a wise Creator; deviation from that nature is forbidden and leads to ruin and divine anger.
rows.anchor: The Qur’ān has not only based its morality but also the whole of religion on nature and since this nature is made by a wise creator

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because environment and misuse of human authority can distort people’s natural guidance, God clarifies it through prophets and books so all can find the path to success and His pleasure.
rows.anchor: the Almighty has explicated all the details of guidance found in human nature through His prophets and books

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Luqmān is cited as evidence because he reflected on life’s realities and was respected by the Qur’an’s opponents; the sūrah also presents familiar inner and outer arguments in a new style.
rows.anchor: the person whose wisdom the Arabs were proud of and whose traditions existed in their literature

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wise Book guides people and is a mercy, but only those who preserve and use their natural traits benefit; arrogant preference for opponents’ nonsense brings humiliating punishment.
rows.anchor: only those people will benefit from it who keep alive the traits of their nature and also make use of them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believers alone succeed under God’s certain promise: all creation in the heavens, earth, and between them belongs to Him, so alleged deities should show what they created.
rows.anchor: whatever is in the heavens and the earth and in between them are creatures of God. No one else has any say in it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Luqmān’s counsel matches the wise Book, showing that common sense agrees with the Qur’an and its opponents are fighting human nature.
rows.anchor: he too counseled his on to things which this wise book is counseling them to

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account specially warns fathers who pressure sons to abandon Islam, echoing the warning in 29:8: Luqmān lovingly urged his son toward the same principles.
rows.anchor: There is a special warning in this for people who in those times were oppressing their sons to leave Islam

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Humanity’s inward and outward favors are gifts from God; many dispute monotheism without argument, guidance from a sage or prophet, or light from scripture.
rows.anchor: all internal and external favours enjoyed by man are actually gifts of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When told to follow God’s Book, these people insist on ancestral ways even if their forefathers followed Satan; God’s strong attachment belongs to Book-followers.
rows.anchor: they will continue to follow the ways of their forefathers even if their forefathers followed Satan

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet should ignore the Hypocrites’ opposition campaign and trust God as his helper and protector.
rows.anchor: He should completely ignore the oppositions campaign launched by the Hypocrites. God is the helper and the protector

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 4–6 reform the jāhili customs of ẓihār and adopted children, which contradict reason; opponents’ clamour should not concern Muslims.
rows.anchor: Measures are stated to reform the customs of ẓihār and adopted children found in the Arab jāhiliyyah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These customs are human fabrications, and God intends to cleanse social contradictions and align life with human nature.
rows.anchor: God wants to cleanse the contradictions found in our social life and bring it in line with the right course of human nature

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Adopted children must be attributed to their actual fathers; if a father is unknown, the child is an ally and brother, not a son.
rows.anchor: Muslims are directed to attribute adopted children to their actual fathers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Past adoption practices under jāhiliyyah are forgiven, but after this clarification Muslims may no longer cling to them.
rows.anchor: Whatever has happened till then under the influence of jāhiliyyah has been forgiven by God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet has the greatest status and right in Islamic society; his wives are believers’ mothers, and the nearness of other relatives follows God’s law of kinship.
rows.anchor: The greatest status and right in an Islamic society is that of the Prophet Muḥammad (sws)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Every prophet is bound by a firm covenant to call people to God’s religion without deference or fear of opposition, making his conduct a test of sincerity and a basis for judgment.
rows.anchor: The Almighty has bound each prophet with the firm promise that he should only invite people to the religion of God in all circumstances

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Battle of the Ditch account seeks to deepen trust in God: despite the confederates’ attack and hypocrites’ plots, divine forces helped the Muslims and routed their enemies.
rows.anchor: the Almighty helped Muslims through His divine forces and their enemies were routed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lesson of the Battle of the Ditch is that God will aid Muslims who remain faithful to His religion and sincere companions of His Messenger despite opposition.
rows.anchor: if like this Muslims continue to adhere to the religion of God and remain sincere companions of His Messenger

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After calling Muslims to obey the Prophet as a unit, the sūrah addresses his wives: their relationship gives them high status if they meet its duties and a stern punishment if they defy them.
rows.anchor: the pure wives of the Prophet (sws) are addressed and explained the responsibilities their status entails

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet’s wives must obey and remain loyal to him, spread the Qur’anic guidance he teaches, stay gracefully in their homes, resist hypocrites’ influence, and devote themselves to teaching its law and wisdom.
rows.anchor: Their real obligation is obedience and loyalty to the Prophet (sws) and spreading the radiance of Qur’ānic guidance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: No believing man or woman may object to a matter decided by God and His Messenger, who hold the greatest right over believers.
rows.anchor: no believing man or woman has the right to say anything in a matter decided by God and His Messenger

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zayd could not sustain his marriage to Zaynab and divorced her despite the Prophet’s urging him not to; the account presents this as the course of events before the Prophet’s later proposal.
rows.anchor: Zayd (rta) could not pull along the marriage, and divorced his wife in spite of the Prophet’s insistence not to do so

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hypocrites taunted Zaynab by calling it an outrage that the Prophet had proposed a noble woman for a freed slave; she endured the taunts patiently and gratefully, but Zayd later divorced her on his own judgment.
rows.anchor: men and women among the Hypocrites started taunting Zaynab (rta) by saying that the Prophet (sws) had committed a great oppression

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet’s marriage to Zaynab could heal her grief, but he feared propaganda because Arabs treated adopted sons as real sons; God directed the marriage to abolish that jāhili custom despite the uproar he expected.
rows.anchor: the Almighty directed him to marry Zaynab (rta) by disregarding all these fears so this marriage could eradicate an evil custom of the age of jāhiliyyah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muslims should remember God; the Prophet’s advent is divine mercy that leads them from polytheism and disbelief into faith and religion.
rows.anchor: The advent of the Prophet (sws) is a manifestation of the great mercy of God to them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is God’s witness before creation, gives Paradise to those who accept his testimony and Hell to rejecters, and is a divine caller and lamp of guidance; he must persist despite Hypocrite opposition.
rows.anchor: witness of God’s religion before His creation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All the Prophet’s wives are legally permitted to him, unlike the four-wife restriction on others, though he has distinct limits; the wives should follow God’s ruling and Hypocrites must stop spreading disinformation about them.
rows.anchor: The restriction of four is not meant for him the way it is for others

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People must seek permission before entering the Prophet’s home, and Muslim women should cover when going out so Hypocrites cannot harass them; Hypocrites receive a final warning to desist.
rows.anchor: People are stopped from entering the house of the Prophet (sws) without asking permission

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah concludes by warning that Judgment is near, no one will benefit another, and leaders and followers who went astray will curse one another.
rows.anchor: First, people are reminded of the Day of Judgement that they should not regard it to be far off

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hypocrites should stop blindly following Jews who harassed Moses; God gave Moses an honorable death and cursed those who harassed him.
rows.anchor: The Hypocrites are warned to give up blindly following the Jews who had harassed Moses (sws) at every step

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They should fear God and obey; God will set their deeds right and forgive their sins, which is the path to great success.
rows.anchor: They should keep fearing God and adopt the attitude of “we listened and we obeyed.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human beings alone were deemed worthy of God’s trust and covenant; their dignity depends on it, and fulfilling its obligation raises them to the highest status.
rows.anchor: only human beings were considered worthy of among all creation of God
